groups.text: One coroutine reads payment ids from a batch, fast.
Another settles each one, which takes one hundred milliseconds.
How does the reader hand ids to the settler?
Put a channel between them: a queue with room for two.
send puts an id in, and receive takes one out.
The settler is already waiting, so id one goes straight to it.
Ids two and three wait in the two spots.
Now the reader sends id four, and both spots are full.
What happens to the reader?
It suspends. send waits for room, and the thread is free to run other coroutines.
When the settler finishes id one and takes id two, a spot opens, and the reader goes on.
So the fast reader now runs at the settler's pace: one id every one hundred milliseconds.
And when the queue is empty, it's receive that suspends, until an id arrives.
When the reader is done, it closes the channel.
The settler's loop ends after the last id.
Forget close, and the settler waits forever.
The default channel has no spots at all.
Each send waits until a receiver takes the id from its hand.
Channels chain into pipelines.
Four workers receive from one channel.
Each id goes to exactly one of them, so at most four settle calls run at once.
Their receipts go into a second channel, which one loop reads.
Sometimes you want whichever answer comes first.
Ask two acquirers for a quote, and let select wait on both.
North needs three hundred milliseconds, east needs one hundred twenty.
Which quote does select return?
East's. select takes the first clause that is ready and drops the rest.
Stopping the loser is your job, so cancel north.
A timeout clause gives a default if nobody answers in five hundred milliseconds.
This is Kotlin only.
A channel with room for two, a sender that closes it, and a loop that receives.
So a channel hands each element to exactly one receiver.
send suspends when it's full, receive suspends when it's empty, and select takes whichever clause is ready first.
Quick check. A rendezvous channel, a fast sender, and a receiver that needs one hundred milliseconds per element.
How often does send return?
